title: New monastics
hookLine: people living near the poor with daily prayer and shared meals

lines: A ROW HOUSE, A SHARED KITCHEN.
cards: A row house on a block where cars rarely slow down. Inside, a handful of people share a kitchen, a budget and a prayer schedule. Before work, they pray around the table.
In the evening the door is open, and a neighbor wanders in for soup and stays to talk. Nobody wears a habit. Nobody lives behind a wall.
But they keep a rule, pray at set hours and share what they have, and they chose to live on this block on purpose, close to people who are struggling. Some people call them new monastics.

teach.h: A RULE, THE HOURS, A SHARED TABLE.
teach.b: This block of the path has spent days with the old monastic families: Benedict's rule, the hours, the shared work.
New monastics take that shape, a rule, set times of prayer, a common table, and plant it in ordinary neighborhoods instead of behind a cloister wall.
They point back to the church's first days in Acts: "And all that believed were together, and had all things common."
Two chapters later Luke says it again: they "were of one heart and of one soul," and none of them called what he had his own. The other text they lean on is older.

When the people of Judah were carried off to Babylon, other prophets were promising a quick return. Jeremiah sent them a letter instead: "Build ye houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens, and eat the fruit of them."

teach.h: SEEK THE PEACE OF THE CITY.
teach.b: And then: "seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace."
The Hebrew word for peace there is shalom: wholeness, well-being. Settle in. Pray for the place.
Your good is tied up with its good. Christians talk about the label in different ways. For some monks and nuns, monastic means vows and a monastery, and they'd keep the word for that.

New monastics say they're borrowing old wisdom, not replacing it, and some keep close friendships with monasteries. Either way, the picture is plain: prayer, a table, and neighbors who come to dinner.

how: New monastic communities share a house or live near one another in struggling neighborhoods, keep a common rule with morning and evening prayer, share meals and resources, and open their tables to neighbors; members come from Protestant, Catholic and other churches.

games.q: you've been carried off to Babylon, far from home. a letter arrives from the prophet Jeremiah. what does it tell you to do?
o: keep your bags packed; you'll be home soon.
build houses, plant gardens, and seek the peace of the city.
keep to yourselves and pray against the city.
games.why: Jeremiah tells them to settle in and pray for the city: "for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace."

practice: Bring to mind the people around you, next door, across the hall, down the street, and let one of them come forward. Set a simple table for them in your mind: soup, bread or takeout on paper plates, and where you'd sit.
If you pray, pray for that neighbor by name, and for the peace of your street; if not, simply wish them well.

wordCard.voice: New monastics. Christians who keep a rule of daily prayer and shared meals in ordinary neighborhoods, often near people who are struggling.

orig.note: Hebrew: peace, wholeness, well-being. The word in Jeremiah 29:7, the peace of the city.

carryVoice: Your line: monks among us. A rule, a table, an open door. See you tomorrow.
